paper_content.abstract: The non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), an exotic phenomenon of localization at the boundary, has recently drawn extensive attention and Floquet engineering offers a powerful approach to expanding its scope. The fundamental role of harmonic response in Floquet systems has nonetheless yet to be elucidated. Here, we introduce the concept of harmonic NHSE and demonstrate it experimentally in an acoustic platform. Within our theoretical framework, we demonstrate that incorporating dynamic couplings into the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model causes a single-frequency input to generate multiple harmonics with diverse skin morphologies, each dictated by the underlying spectral winding topology at its respective frequency. Experimentally, we implement the requisite dynamic couplings in an acoustic lattice via programmable unidirectional couplers. By simply reconfiguring the excitation and modulation frequencies, we demonstrate controllable switching of unipolar and bipolar harmonic NHSEs, which exhibit uniform and opposite sound gathering toward the sample boundaries, respectively. By introducing the class of harmonic NHSE, our work sets the stage for further investigating non-Hermitian physics with harmonic effects.
paper_content.introduction:
Non-Hermitian systems, typically featuring asymmetric couplings and gain/loss, have garnered extensive attention owing to their unique phenomena and broad applications beyond Hermitian regimes1–3. In particular, the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), referring to the accumulation of bulk states at the lattice boundary, has emerged as a cornerstone of non-Hermitian physics4–6. Over the past few years, a number of theoretical frameworks, such as the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ), Bloch spectral winding and dynamical degeneracy splitting, have been developed to characterize the NHSE and its related topological properties7–14. These advances have propelled the experimental observation of diverse NHSE morphologies across photonic15, circuit16,17, acoustic18–21, mechanical22,23, quantum walk24, and ultracold atom25,26 platforms, paving the way for potential applications in optical funneling15, robust directional transport27, and non-Hermitian lasing28.

Floquet engineering, an established approach for tailoring material properties via time-periodic modulation29–31, has recently been extended to non-Hermitian systems. This development has led to richer phenomena, including non-Hermitian Floquet topological states32–34, multiple phase transitions35,36, and Floquet exceptional points37,38. In particular, a periodically driven system can exhibit Floquet NHSE even when the instantaneous Hamiltonian at each step lacks NHSE38–43. Along with breaking the bulk-boundary correspondence, Floquet NHSE enables the relocation of topological edge states to a single boundary or the separation of distinct edge states at opposite boundaries, giving rise to the Floquet skin-topological effect40,41. In these studies, the key roles played by Floquet engineering are breaking time-reversal symmetry and introducing artificial gauge fields (or complex long-range couplings). Despite these advances, however, the implications of harmonic generation—a fundamental feature of Floquet systems—has yet to be explored in the context of NHSE. The primary reasons are twofold. Theoretically, most studies focus on the stroboscopic dynamics governed by the effective Hamiltonian38–40; the higher-order Floquet states (harmonics), which share the same eigen-properties with the zeroth-order one, are typically disregarded. Experimentally, Floquet NHSE has so far been implemented in waveguide and ring resonator systems, where spatial modulation emulates temporal periodicity41–43; such setups inherently exclude harmonic generation due to their time-invariant nature.

Here, we introduce and experimentally observe a new type of NHSE, dubbed harmonic NHSE, in Floquet non-Hermitian lattices. This phenomenon results from a direct synergy between Floquet engineering and non-Hermitian topology—time-periodic driving generates a spectrum of harmonics in open-boundary lattices, while the skin localization of each harmonic is dictated by the spectral winding topology at its own frequency. The concept is demonstrated through a simple Hatano-Nelson (HN) model44 incorporating time-periodic couplings. In addition to the unipolar harmonic NHSE induced by uniform spectral winding, more intriguingly, as sketched in Fig. 1, the harmonics can exhibit bipolar NHSE in a long-range lattice with twisted winding spectrum, despite the extended nature of the fundamental wave. Experimentally, we design two nonreciprocal acoustic lattices to observe these harmonic NHSEs, with both dynamic and nonreciprocal couplings reconfigurable via active unidirectional couplers. By tuning the excitation and modulation frequencies, we clearly demonstrate the ability of selectively localizing different harmonics, with their weights flexibly controllable by simply adjusting the duty ratio of dynamic couplings. These results not only extend the existing NHSE framework but also open new avenues for harmonic wave manipulation.

Given the real-space Hamiltonian H r (t) for an N-site finite lattice with open boundaries, the response to a monochromatic excitation at frequency f 0 is described by (see Methods):

(Δ 0 +mΩ) Q m + Δ 1 Q m-1 + Δ -1 Q m+1 = P m (1)

where Δ m = T 1 T 0 H k (t)ei2mπΩtdt is the mth-order Fourier component of H k (t), with Ω = 1/T denoting the modulation frequency. In particular, Δ 0 = T 1 T 0 H k (t)dt = H(cid:2) k denotes the time-averaged Hamiltonian. The spectrum of H k under periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) comprises infinitely many branches, each shifted by Ω, as a result of the unitary transformation UyH k U = diag(H(cid:2) k+mΩ, ..., H(cid:2) k+Ω, H(cid:2) k, H(cid:2) k-Ω, ..., H(cid:2) k-mΩ)45. Due to the single-band nature of our model, these spectral branches remain non-interacting even when they overlap, unlike in two- or multi-band cases46. Specifically, the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k corresponds to that of H(cid:2) k - mΩ, and its winding topology governs the NHSE under open boundary conditions (OBCs) within the associated Floquet replica.

Moreover, as demonstrated above, the NHSE within the mth-order Floquet replica is governed by the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently by the spectrum of H(cid:2) k - mΩ. Consequently, the harmonic NHSE under realistic excitation can be fully characterized by examining solely the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently, the spectrum of H(cid:2) k for single-band models. (Remarkably, for two- or multi-band models, the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k can differ fundamentally from the spectrum of H(cid:2) k, due to the interaction between different Floquet branches upon closing46). The above theoretical framework provides a general route to account for harmonic effects in Floquet non-Hermitian systems.

First, we introduce time-periodic dynamic couplings into a prototypical static HN lattice44, forming a Floquet HN (FHN) lattice (see Fig. 2a). The Bloch Hamiltonian of the FHN lattice is H k (t) = κ L + κ D (t) eik + κ R + κ D (t) e-ik. Physically, the nonreciprocal static couplings κ L and κ R establish the fundamental NHSE, while the reciprocal dynamic couplings κ D (t) contribute to the harmonic generation. For simplicity, we assume κ D (t) = κ 0 cos(2πΩt), as it couples only Floquet harmonics of adjacent orders without introducing any additional static component. As shown in Fig. 2b, both the spectrum of H(cid:2) k and the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k form a counterclockwise loop in the complex frequency plane. A reference frequency f b enclosed by the spectrum f(k) carries a nontrivial spectral winding number and their associated NHSEs. Specifically, when choosing the excitation frequency f 0 = 0 and modulation frequency Ω = 1.5, the fundamental frequency f 0 lies at the Bloch-like point of the spectrum, while the +1st- and -1st-order harmonic frequencies f +1 and f -1 fall within the counterclockwise and clockwise spectral loops, respectively (see Fig. 2e). Protected by the twisted winding topology, the incident fundamental wave maintains an extended spatial distribution, whereas the +1st- and -1st-order harmonics undergo unidirectional accumulation toward the left and right boundaries, respectively, as shown in Fig. 2f. Notably, the extended nature at the Bloch-like point can be interpreted in terms of both the vanishing spectral winding number and the specific GBZ with purely real Bloch wave vectors4,8. Furthermore, different harmonics can be selectively engineered to exhibit distinct skin and evanescent behaviors by tuning f 0 and Ω, as detailed in Supplementary Note 2.

We further achieve control over the harmonic intensity distribution by tuning the duty ratio R of dynamic couplings. Since the Fourier components of the dynamic couplings determine the conversion between harmonics, varying R effectively modulates their magnitudes and thereby tailors the intensity weights of individual harmonics within the lattice. This controllability is readily implemented by leveraging the flexible tunability of the real-time unidirectional couplers in our experiments. To ensure that the PBC spectra of time-averaged Hamiltonians (and hence the harmonic NHSE) remain quantitatively unchanged during variation of R, we keep the zeroth-order Fourier component of κ D constant, namely, Rκ 0 = κ(cid:2). Under this condition, the coefficient of the leading order (±1st) Fourier component of κ D is given by c ±1 = ±κ(cid:2)sinc(πR), whose absolute value decreases monotonically with increasing R in the interval [0, 1]. Specifically, when R approaches zero, c ±1 reaches its maximum value κ(cid:2); when R approaches one, c ±1 decreases to its minimum value zero.

Eigenvalue problem of the Floquet non-Hermitian lattice

The Bloch Hamiltonian H k (t) of the Floquet non-Hermitian lattice is governed by the Schrödinger equation:

-i d/dt |ψ(t) > = 2πH k (t) |ψ(t) > (5)

The Floquet state solutions to this equation take the Floquet form:

|ψ(t) > = e-i2πϵt |u(t) > (6)

where |u(t + T) > = |u(t) > is the time-periodic Floquet mode, and ϵ is the quasi-energy. Substituting Equation (6) into Equation (5) yields:

2πϵ |u(t) > = 2πH k (t) + i d/dt |u(t) > (7)

Specifically, |u(t) > can be expanded as a Fourier series:

|u(t) > = Σ m |u m > e-i2πmΩt (8)

where |u m > are the Fourier components. Similarly, the Hamiltonian H k (t) can be expanded as:

H k (t) = Σ m Δ m e-i2πmΩt (9)

where Δ m = T 1 T 0 H k (t)ei2mπΩtdt is the mth-order Fourier component of H k (t). Substituting Equations (8) and (9) into Equation (7) and regrouping terms, we obtain a time-independent eigenvalue problem in the frequency domain:

ϵ |u j > = H k |u j > (10)

where the time-independent Floquet mode is |u j > = [..., |a -m >, ..., |a -1 >, |a 0 >, |a +1 >, ..., |a +m >]T, with the subscripts denoting the Floquet order. The time-independent Hamiltonian H k takes the form:

Note that, in practical calculations, we truncate the infinite-dimensional H k at a sufficiently high order of harmonics (m = ±5), ensuring the eigenvalue problem can be numerically solved.

Excitation problem of the Floquet non-Hermitian lattice. For an N-site Floquet non-Hermitian lattice described by the real-space Hamiltonian H r (t), the system’s dynamics under excitation is governed by the nonhomogeneous Schrödinger equation:

-i d/dt Q(t) = 2πH r (t) Q(t) + P(t) (12)

where

P(t) = 2πe-i2πf 0 t [δ 1s, δ 2s, ..., δ ns, ..., δ Ns]T (13)

represents a time-domain excitation at a specific site n = s with monochromatic frequency f 0, and Q(t) represents the time-domain response across all sites. H r (t) and Q(t) can be written as Fourier series:

H r (t) = Σ m Δ m e-i2πmΩt (14)

Q(t) = Σ m Q m e-i2π(f 0+mΩ)t (15)

where Δ m = T 1 T 0 H r (t)ei2mπΩtdt is the mth-order Fourier component of H r (t). Inserting Equations (14) and (15) into Equation (12), and using the orthogonality properties of Fourier harmonics: e-i2πmΩt, e-i2πm0Ωt = δ mm0, we get

(See Equation 16 in original text)

where ζ m = f 0 + mΩ denotes the mth-order harmonic frequency generated by the monochromatic excitation, Q m = [a 1 m, a 2 m, ..., a n m, ..., a N m]T represents the frequency-domain response of the mth-order harmonic across the lattice, P m = 2π [δ m0 δ 1s, δ m0 δ 2s, ..., δ m0 δ ns, ..., δ m0 δ Ns]T describes the excitation applied at sites. Notably, only the component with m = 0 and n = s satisfies δ m0 δ ns = 1, while all other components vanish. This reflects the fact that, in realistic settings, only the zeroth-order harmonic component at site s can be directly excited.

Experimental setup and measurements. Our experimental cavity-tube sample (shown in Figs. 3a and 4a) is fabricated using 3D printing with acoustically rigid photosensitive resin, featuring a wall thickness of 2.0 mm and a fabrication tolerance of 0.1 mm. Each air-filled cavity, having a height of h = 43.0 mm, a width of w = 28.0 mm, and a length of l = 28.0 mm, supports a dipole mode with resonant frequency ω 0 ≈ 4000 Hz and intrinsic loss γ 0 ≈ 38 Hz. Adjacent cavities are connected by two narrow tubes, each having a length of y = 19.8 mm and a cross-sectional area of A = 6.4 × 6.4 mm2. These tubes generate a reciprocal acoustic coupling of κ N ≈ 75 Hz. At both the top and bottom surfaces of each cavity, five holes are drilled for inserting the loudspeakers and microphones. The holes are sealed when not in use to prevent acoustic leakage. The unidirectional dynamic (or static) couplings between cavities are implemented using real-time unidirectional couplers, each consisting of a microphone, a preamplifier (Type LM386), a voltage-controlled amplifier (Type VCA810), a phase shifter (Type MCP41010), and a loudspeaker. The gain factor of the voltage-controlled amplifier is modulated in real time by a signal generator (Aigtek Type ATA-214). When the signal generator outputs a square-wave signal, the real-time unidirectional couplers realize square-form dynamic unidirectional couplings κ D, alternating between a high level of κ 0 and a low level of 0. For the experiments presented in Figs. 3 and 4, κ 0 is tuned to approximately 120 Hz and 56 Hz, respectively. In addition, when the signal generator outputs a direct current signal, the real-time unidirectional couplers realize static unidirectional couplings κ R ≈ -28 Hz for the experiment in Fig. 4. The values of the above acoustic parameters are calibrated from independent measurements of a binary-cavity unit (or a ternary-cavity unit) with a single real-time unidirectional coupler (see details in Supplementary Note 4). In each measurement, the sound signal is launched from a loudspeaker driven by the output generator module of an audio analyzer (B&K Type 3160-A-042). The sound pressure response is measured with a detector microphone (B&K Type 4958) and processed with the signal acquisition module of the audio analyzer.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript reports a novel class of non-Hermitian skin effects (NHSEs), termed the harmonic NHSE, which emerges from the intricate interplay between the characteristic harmonic generation in Floquet systems and the unique NHSE in non- Hermitian systems. The authors demonstrate that the NHSEs of different frequency harmonics are governed by the zeroth- order Floquet spectral topology, leading to distinct localizations across these harmonics. They illustrate this discovery using two modified Hatano-Nelson models with dynamic modulations, wherein unidirectional spectral winding produces unipolar harmonic NHSE, while twisted winding gives rise to bipolar harmonic NHSE. Experimentally, the harmonic NHSE is observed in an array of acoustic cavities with genuine time modulation. By tuning the excitation and modulation frequencies, the authors clearly demonstrate the selective localization and controllable weights of different harmonics.
In my view, the NHSE associated with harmonic generation in Floquet non-Hermitian systems represents a previously unexplored regime. While several studies have proposed the concept of Floquet NHSE, the role of harmonics has never been addressed, either theoretically or experimentally. This work identifies the critical gap and uncovers novel physics. From the perspective of innovation, this work is timely and groundbreaking, tackling an untapped topic. Regarding the results, the authors provide extensive details in both theoretical analysis and experimental approaches. Overall, the manuscript is clearly organized and well written, I would like to recommend its publication if the following questions are well addressed.
1. In the theoretical model in Fig. 2, both nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor non-reciprocal couplings are considered. Would longer-range non-reciprocal couplings lead to richer behaviors in harmonic NHSE?
2. What is the specific definition of the spectral winding number used in this work? Could the authors provide it explicitly? How to distinguish harmonic NHSE from the Floquet-induced NHSE?
3. Could the presence of loss in experiments affect the observation of harmonic NHSE? What are the main sources of loss?
4. In the experiments shown in Fig. 5, why is the lower limit of the duty ratio R set to 0.4? Is there a specific consideration for this choice?
5. How universal is this control mechanism? Does it persist for sinusoidal (rather than square-wave) modulation, or in systems with stronger dissipation?
6. Compared to conventional Floquet NHSE, does harmonic NHSE will show unique dynamic characteristics?
7. For multi-band models, does the coupling between different Floquet branches lead to phenomena distinct from those in single-band models, or affect the formation of the Harmonic NHSE? Can the topological phases still be distinguished by the low-order Floquet spectrum of the Hamiltonian Hk? Does it introduce new topological phenomena? Please provide a brief discussion.
8. In figure3c, 4b, only s21 and s31 are considered to extract the coupling strength. If s12/s21,s13/s31 are all considered, can the coupling still fit well with the experiment data?
9. How about the energy distribution at the other frequencies? Can you provide the spectra response at single stie (at edge / middle of the model)?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This submitted manuscript by Zhang et al. presented a novel and compelling study on the topic of harmonic non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). The authors successfully bridged the fields of time-dependent Floquet engineering and non-Hermitian topology by introducing the harmonic waves, which were experimentally generated by time-periodic driving. The distinct and controllable skin effect morphologies were then exhibited. Overall, I think the concept is innovative, the theoretical framework is solid, and the experimental realization in an acoustic platform with real-time modulations is impressive and provides clear, convincing evidence. This work may open a new direction in the study of dynamic non-Hermitian systems and is likely to be of significant interest to the broader physics community. I believe this paper is well-suited for publication in Nature Communications after the following suggested revisions are addressed.
1. The main text presented simulated results. It would be beneficial for the authors to describe the simulation methods, particularly explaining how the active unidirectional couplers were realized in the simulations.
2. I am interested in several experimental details. Specifically, more information on the feed-back microphones and loudspeakers (such as types or models) used for the real-time unidirectional couplers. Additionally, how to ensure the consistent performance characteristics of these compact acoustic components?
3. In the Supplementary Information Note 3, the authors employed the transmission amplitude spectra |(cid:1)_21| and |(cid:1)_31| to fit the relevant parameters. Since it is challenging to directly measure the acoustic pressure at the source, I am interested in the measurement methodology for the individual transmission coefficients. Additionally, the fitting equation in Eq. (S6) differs from the one used in the authors' prior work (10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.017201). Could the authors elaborate on the consideration behind this modification in the methodology please?
4. Other minor suggestions:
4.1 Some figure captions (e.g., Figs. 2, 4) are very dense with parameter lists. Consider moving some of these details to the main text or methods for improved readability.
4.2 On Page 7, lines 128-130, the text "...the +1st- and −1st-order harmonics undergo unidirectional accumulation toward the right and left boundaries, respectively..." seems to contradict the caption of Fig. 2f, which states the +1st harmonic goes left and the -1st goes right. Please verify and correct this for consistency.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, Zhang et al. introduce and experimentally demonstrate the concept of a "harmonic non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE)" in a Floquet-engineered acoustic lattice. The core idea is that when a monochromatic wave excites a time-periodically modulated non-Hermitian lattice, it can generate multiple harmonics, each of which can exhibit a distinct skin localization phenotype—unipolar or bipolar—dictated by the spectral winding topology at its respective frequency. The authors provide a theoretical framework based on a frequency-domain analysis and present compelling experimental evidence using a reconfigurable acoustic platform with active, real-time modulations. The ability to selectively control and spatially separate different harmonic components via a single-frequency excitation is a key experimental achievement.
I find this work to be of high quality, timely, and highly suitable for publication in Nature Communications. The concept of "harmonic NHSE" is novel and represents a significant extension of the non-Hermitian skin effect into the realm of Floquet systems with genuine time modulation. The study successfully bridges a gap in the field by focusing on the harmonic generation aspect, which is a fundamental feature of Floquet systems but had been overlooked in previous studies of Floquet NHSE, particularly those relying on synthetic dimensions (e.g., waveguide arrays). The combination of a clear theoretical proposal with a sophisticated and convincing experimental demonstration in acoustics is a major strength. The observation of both unipolar and, more impressively, bipolar harmonic NHSE, where different harmonics localize at opposite ends of the system, is a striking result. The findings are likely to stimulate immediate interest across various platforms in photonics, circuit QED, and cold atoms.
I am therefore strongly in favor of publication, provided that the authors can address the following points to further enhance the clarity and theoretical rigor of their otherwise excellent manuscript.
1. GBZ Calculation for Floquet Model: The topological origin of the skin effect for each harmonic is central to the present approach. To make this connection more transparent and rigorous, I encourage the authors to calculate and present the Generalized Brillouin Zone (GBZ) for their Floquet model, following the established non-Bloch band theory (e.g., Yao and Wang, PRL, 2018). Demonstrating how the GBZ and the associated complex wavevectors dictate the skin localization direction for the fundamental wave and its harmonics would significantly strengthen the topological foundation of the "harmonic NHSE" concept.
2. Clarification on the Extended Nature of the Zeroth Harmonic (f₀): In Figure 1 and the corresponding discussion of the bipolar NHSE, the zeroth-order harmonic (f₀) is depicted as extended. This appears counterintuitive because the underlying static lattice, with its nonreciprocal static hoppings (κ_L, κ_R), should itself exhibit clear features of NHSE, localizing all eigenstates. The authors should provide a clearer explanation for this observation. Is this extended behavior a result of a specific parameter choice (e.g., f₀ being exactly at a Bloch-like point in the spectrum)? A detailed discussion on why f₀ resists skin localization in this specific scenario, while the system remains non-Hermitian, is necessary to resolve this apparent contradiction for the reader.
3. Justification for the Excitation Problem Framework: The authors state that "the harmonic NHSE can be adequately characterized by focusing solely on the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of mathcal{H}_k, or equivalently, the spectrum of Ḥ_k", justifying this by the orthogonality of Fourier harmonics in the excitation vector P_m. While this simplification is crucial for the analysis, the reasoning provided is somewhat obscure. I find it difficult to fully grasp why the topology of the time-averaged Hamiltonian \bar{H}_k alone determines the skin effect for all higher harmonics generated in the excitation problem. The authors should elaborate on this point, perhaps with a more detailed derivation or a physical argument in the Methods or Supplementary Information, to clarify the validity of this approach.

Reply: The control mechanism of Floquet modulation is universal and can be, in principle,
reconfigured to realize arbitrary forms of dynamic coupling, including the sinusoidal one. This
reconfigurability originates from the working principle of our real-time unidirectional coupler: the
sound signal in a cavity is collected by a microphone, then modulated through a preamplifier, a
voltage-controlled amplifier, and a phase shifter, before being output into another cavity via a
loudspeaker. In particular, the gain factor of the voltage-controlled amplifier is controlled in real
time by a waveform generator. Therefore, to achieve sinusoidal Floquet modulation, one simply
needs to replace the square-wave signal with a sinusoidal one. Remarkably, we employ square-
wave modulation in our work because of its simplicity and ease of experimental implementation.
Moreover, the Floquet modulation mechanism is independent of dissipation. As long as a steady
state can be established in the system, the Floquet modulation mechanism remains valid.

the broader physics community. I believe this paper is well-suited for publication in Nature
Communications after the following suggested revisions are addressed.

In this manuscript, Zhang et al. introduce and experimentally demonstrate the concept of a
"harmonic non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE)" in a Floquet-engineered acoustic lattice. The core idea
is that when a monochromatic wave excites a time-periodically modulated non-Hermitian lattice,
it can generate multiple harmonics, each of which can exhibit a distinct skin localization
phenotype—unipolar or bipolar—dictated by the spectral winding topology at its respective
frequency. The authors provide a theoretical framework based on a frequency-domain analysis and
present compelling experimental evidence using a reconfigurable acoustic platform with active,
real-time modulations. The ability to selectively control and spatially separate different harmonic
components via a single-frequency excitation is a key experimental achievement.
I find this work to be of high quality, timely, and highly suitable for publication in Nature
Communications. The concept of "harmonic NHSE" is novel and represents a significant extension
of the non-Hermitian skin effect into the realm of Floquet systems with genuine time modulation.
The study successfully bridges a gap in the field by focusing on the harmonic generation aspect,
which is a fundamental feature of Floquet systems but had been overlooked in previous studies of
Floquet NHSE, particularly those relying on synthetic dimensions (e.g., waveguide arrays). The
combination of a clear theoretical proposal with a sophisticated and convincing experimental
demonstration in acoustics is a major strength. The observation of both unipolar and, more
impressively, bipolar harmonic NHSE, where different harmonics localize at opposite ends of the
system, is a striking result. The findings are likely to stimulate immediate interest across various
platforms in photonics, circuit QED, and cold atoms.
I am therefore strongly in favor of publication, provided that the authors can address the following
points to further enhance the clarity and theoretical rigor of their otherwise excellent manuscript.

Reply: This is an insightful question. First, we confirm that the zeroth-order harmonic f₀ in bipolar
harmonic NHSE is indeed chosen to lie exactly at a Bloch-like point of the spectrum. Below we
explain why a Bloch-like point corresponds to an extended state despite the underlying
nonreciprocal couplings. In simple settings such as the Hatano–Nelson model with nearest-
neighbor nonreciprocal couplings, all eigenstates localize toward the direction of the dominant
coupling, giving the well-known unipolar NHSE [Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 570 (1996)]. However, in more
complex settings—e.g., when long-range nonreciprocal couplings are introduced—the situation
becomes richer. Besides the majority of eigenstates that exhibit leftward and rightward NHSE
(bipolar NHSE), there can exist isolated extended eigenstates, whose eigenenergies exactly
correspond to the Bloch-like points [Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 246801 (2019); Phys. Rev. Res. 1, 023013
(2019)]. These points and the associated bipolar NHSE defy the oversimplified picture in which all
eigenstates localize toward the dominant hopping direction. These Bloch-like extended states can
be understood from two complementary perspectives. 1) Spectral winding perspective: A Bloch-
like point is an eigenenergy at which the periodic boundary condition (PBC) spectrum intersects
the open boundary condition (OBC) spectrum (see Fig. R5a). Its PBC spectral winding number is
therefore zero, unlike the majority of eigenenergies that carry a nonzero winding number.
According to the topological origin of the NHSE [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 086801 (2020); Phys. Rev. Lett.
125, 126402 (2020)], only eigenstates associated with nonzero winding undergo skin localization.
The Bloch-like eigenstate, having zero winding, remains extended. 2) GBZ perspective: At a Bloch-
like point, the GBZ intersects the unit circle, meaning that the corresponding Bloch wave vector is
purely real (see Fig. R5b). As a result, the wave function is spatially extended [Phys. Rev. Lett. 121,
086803 (2018)]. In contrast, the bipolar NHSE emerges because points inside (outside) the unit
circle correspond to exponential localization toward the left (right) boundary.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), an exotic phenomenon of localization at the boundary, has recently drawn extensive attention and Floquet engineering offers a powerful approach to expanding its scope. The fundamental role of harmonic response in Floquet systems has nonetheless yet to be elucidated. Here, we introduce the concept of harmonic NHSE and demonstrate it experimentally in an acoustic platform. Within our theoretical framework, we demonstrate that incorporating dynamic couplings into the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model causes a single-frequency input to generate multiple harmonics with diverse skin morphologies, each dictated by the underlying spectral winding topology at its respective frequency. Experimentally, we implement the requisite dynamic couplings in an acoustic lattice via programmable unidirectional couplers. By simply reconfiguring the excitation and modulation frequencies, we demonstrate controllable switching of unipolar and bipolar harmonic NHSEs, which exhibit uniform and opposite sound gathering toward the sample boundaries, respectively. By introducing the class of harmonic NHSE, our work sets the stage for further investigating non-Hermitian physics with harmonic effects.

---

## Introduction

Non-Hermitian systems, typically featuring asymmetric couplings and gain/loss, have garnered extensive attention owing to their unique phenomena and broad applications beyond Hermitian regimes1–3. In particular, the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), referring to the accumulation of bulk states at the lattice boundary, has emerged as a cornerstone of non-Hermitian physics4–6. Over the past few years, a number of theoretical frameworks, such as the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ), Bloch spectral winding and dynamical degeneracy splitting, have been developed to characterize the NHSE and its related topological properties7–14. These advances have propelled the experimental observation of diverse NHSE morphologies across photonic15, circuit16,17, acoustic18–21, mechanical22,23, quantum walk24, and ultracold atom25,26 platforms, paving the way for potential applications in optical funneling15, robust directional transport27, and non-Hermitian lasing28.

Floquet engineering, an established approach for tailoring material properties via time-periodic modulation29–31, has recently been extended to non-Hermitian systems. This development has led to richer phenomena, including non-Hermitian Floquet topological states32–34, multiple phase transitions35,36, and Floquet exceptional points37,38. In particular, a periodically driven system can exhibit Floquet NHSE even when the instantaneous Hamiltonian at each step lacks NHSE38–43. Along with breaking the bulk-boundary correspondence, Floquet NHSE enables the relocation of topological edge states to a single boundary or the separation of distinct edge states at opposite boundaries, giving rise to the Floquet skin-topological effect40,41. In these studies, the key roles played by Floquet engineering are breaking time-reversal symmetry and introducing artificial gauge fields (or complex long-range couplings). Despite these advances, however, the implications of harmonic generation—a fundamental feature of Floquet systems—has yet to be explored in the context of NHSE. The primary reasons are twofold. Theoretically, most studies focus on the stroboscopic dynamics governed by the effective Hamiltonian38–40; the higher-order Floquet states (harmonics), which share the same eigen-properties with the zeroth-order one, are typically disregarded. Experimentally, Floquet NHSE has so far been implemented in waveguide and ring resonator systems, where spatial modulation emulates temporal periodicity41–43; such setups inherently exclude harmonic generation due to their time-invariant nature.

Here, we introduce and experimentally observe a new type of NHSE, dubbed harmonic NHSE, in Floquet non-Hermitian lattices. This phenomenon results from a direct synergy between Floquet engineering and non-Hermitian topology—time-periodic driving generates a spectrum of harmonics in open-boundary lattices, while the skin localization of each harmonic is dictated by the spectral winding topology at its own frequency. The concept is demonstrated through a simple Hatano-Nelson (HN) model44 incorporating time-periodic couplings. In addition to the unipolar harmonic NHSE induced by uniform spectral winding, more intriguingly, as sketched in Fig. 1, the harmonics can exhibit bipolar NHSE in a long-range lattice with twisted winding spectrum, despite the extended nature of the fundamental wave. Experimentally, we design two nonreciprocal acoustic lattices to observe these harmonic NHSEs, with both dynamic and nonreciprocal couplings reconfigurable via active unidirectional couplers. By tuning the excitation and modulation frequencies, we clearly demonstrate the ability of selectively localizing different harmonics, with their weights flexibly controllable by simply adjusting the duty ratio of dynamic couplings. These results not only extend the existing NHSE framework but also open new avenues for harmonic wave manipulation.

---

## Results

In contrast to the above eigenvalue problem, in practice, one needs to consider an excitation problem to identify the harmonic NHSE. Given the real-space Hamiltonian H r (t) for an N-site finite lattice with open boundaries, the response to a monochromatic excitation at frequency f 0 is described by (see Methods):

(Δ 0 +mΩ) Q m + Δ 1 Q m-1 + Δ -1 Q m+1 = P m (1)

where Δ m = T 1 T 0 H k (t)ei2mπΩtdt is the mth-order Fourier component of H k (t), with Ω = 1/T denoting the modulation frequency. In particular, Δ 0 = T 1 T 0 H k (t)dt = H(cid:2) k denotes the time-averaged Hamiltonian. The spectrum of H k under periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) comprises infinitely many branches, each shifted by Ω, as a result of the unitary transformation UyH k U = diag(H(cid:2) k+mΩ, ..., H(cid:2) k+Ω, H(cid:2) k, H(cid:2) k-Ω, ..., H(cid:2) k-mΩ)45. Due to the single-band nature of our model, these spectral branches remain non-interacting even when they overlap, unlike in two- or multi-band cases46. Specifically, the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k corresponds to that of H(cid:2) k - mΩ, and its winding topology governs the NHSE under open boundary conditions (OBCs) within the associated Floquet replica.

Moreover, as demonstrated above, the NHSE within the mth-order Floquet replica is governed by the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently by the spectrum of H(cid:2) k - mΩ. Consequently, the harmonic NHSE under realistic excitation can be fully characterized by examining solely the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently, the spectrum of H(cid:2) k for single-band models. (Remarkably, for two- or multi-band models, the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k can differ fundamentally from the spectrum of H(cid:2) k, due to the interaction between different Floquet branches upon closing46). The above theoretical framework provides a general route to account for harmonic effects in Floquet non-Hermitian systems.

First, we introduce time-periodic dynamic couplings into a prototypical static HN lattice44, forming a Floquet HN (FHN) lattice (see Fig. 2a). The Bloch Hamiltonian of the FHN lattice is H k (t) = κ L + κ D (t) eik + κ R + κ D (t) e-ik. Physically, the nonreciprocal static couplings κ L and κ R establish the fundamental NHSE, while the reciprocal dynamic couplings κ D (t) contribute to the harmonic generation. For simplicity, we assume κ D (t) = κ 0 cos(2πΩt), as it couples only Floquet harmonics of adjacent orders without introducing any additional static component. As shown in Fig. 2b, both the spectrum of H(cid:2) k and the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k form a counterclockwise loop in the complex frequency plane. A reference frequency f b enclosed by the spectrum f(k) carries a nontrivial spectral winding number and their associated NHSEs. Specifically, when choosing the excitation frequency f 0 = 0 and modulation frequency Ω = 1.5, the fundamental frequency f 0 lies at the Bloch-like point of the spectrum, while the +1st- and -1st-order harmonic frequencies f +1 and f -1 fall within the counterclockwise and clockwise spectral loops, respectively (see Fig. 2e). Protected by the twisted winding topology, the incident fundamental wave maintains an extended spatial distribution, whereas the +1st- and -1st-order harmonics undergo unidirectional accumulation toward the left and right boundaries, respectively, as shown in Fig. 2f. Notably, the extended nature at the Bloch-like point can be interpreted in terms of both the vanishing spectral winding number and the specific GBZ with purely real Bloch wave vectors4,8. Furthermore, different harmonics can be selectively engineered to exhibit distinct skin and evanescent behaviors by tuning f 0 and Ω, as detailed in Supplementary Note 2.

We further achieve control over the harmonic intensity distribution by tuning the duty ratio R of dynamic couplings. Since the Fourier components of the dynamic couplings determine the conversion between harmonics, varying R effectively modulates their magnitudes and thereby tailors the intensity weights of individual harmonics within the lattice. This controllability is readily implemented by leveraging the flexible tunability of the real-time unidirectional couplers in our experiments. To ensure that the PBC spectra of time-averaged Hamiltonians (and hence the harmonic NHSE) remain quantitatively unchanged during variation of R, we keep the zeroth-order Fourier component of κ D constant, namely, Rκ 0 = κ(cid:2). Under this condition, the coefficient of the leading order (±1st) Fourier component of κ D is given by c ±1 = ±κ(cid:2)sinc(πR), whose absolute value decreases monotonically with increasing R in the interval [0, 1]. Specifically, when R approaches zero, c ±1 reaches its maximum value κ(cid:2); when R approaches one, c ±1 decreases to its minimum value zero.

Eigenvalue problem of the Floquet non-Hermitian lattice

The Bloch Hamiltonian H k (t) of the Floquet non-Hermitian lattice is governed by the Schrödinger equation:

Experimental setup and measurements. Our experimental cavity-tube sample (shown in Figs. 3a and 4a) is fabricated using 3D printing with acoustically rigid photosensitive resin, featuring a wall thickness of 2.0 mm and a fabrication tolerance of 0.1 mm. Each air-filled cavity, having a height of h = 43.0 mm, a width of w = 28.0 mm, and a length of l = 28.0 mm, supports a dipole mode with resonant frequency ω 0 ≈ 4000 Hz and intrinsic loss γ 0 ≈ 38 Hz. These tubes generate a reciprocal acoustic coupling of κ N ≈ 75 Hz. At both the top and bottom surfaces of each cavity, five holes are drilled for inserting the loudspeakers and microphones. ## Abstract

The non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), an exotic phenomenon of localization at the boundary, has recently drawn extensive attention and Floquet engineering offers a powerful approach to expanding its scope. The fundamental role of harmonic response in Floquet systems has nonetheless yet to be elucidated. Here, we introduce the concept of harmonic NHSE and demonstrate it experimentally in an acoustic platform. Within our theoretical framework, we demonstrate that incorporating dynamic couplings into the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model causes a single-frequency input to generate multiple harmonics with diverse skin morphologies, each dictated by the underlying spectral winding topology at its respective frequency. ## Introduction

Non-Hermitian systems, typically featuring asymmetric couplings and gain/loss, have garnered extensive attention owing to their unique phenomena and broad applications beyond Hermitian regimes1–3. In particular, the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), referring to the accumulation of bulk states at the lattice boundary, has emerged as a cornerstone of non-Hermitian physics4–6. Over the past few years, a number of theoretical frameworks, such as the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ), Bloch spectral winding and dynamical degeneracy splitting, have been developed to characterize the NHSE and its related topological properties7–14. These advances have propelled the experimental observation of diverse NHSE morphologies across photonic15, circuit16,17, acoustic18–21, mechanical22,23, quantum walk24, and ultracold atom25,26 platforms, paving the way for potential applications in optical funneling15, robust directional transport27, and non-Hermitian lasing28.

Floquet engineering, an established approach for tailoring material properties via time-periodic modulation29–31, has recently been extended to non-Hermitian systems. This development has led to richer phenomena, including non-Hermitian Floquet topological states32–34, multiple phase transitions35,36, and Floquet exceptional points37,38. In particular, a periodically driven system can exhibit Floquet NHSE even when the instantaneous Hamiltonian at each step lacks NHSE38–43. Along with breaking the bulk-boundary correspondence, Floquet NHSE enables the relocation of topological edge states to a single boundary or the separation of distinct edge states at opposite boundaries, giving rise to the Floquet skin-topological effect40,41. In these studies, the key roles played by Floquet engineering are breaking time-reversal symmetry and introducing artificial gauge fields (or complex long-range couplings). Despite these advances, however, the implications of harmonic generation—a fundamental feature of Floquet systems—has yet to be explored in the context of NHSE. The primary reasons are twofold. Theoretically, most studies focus on the stroboscopic dynamics governed by the effective Hamiltonian38–40; the higher-order Floquet states (harmonics), which share the same eigen-properties with the zeroth-order one, are typically disregarded. Experimentally, Floquet NHSE has so far been implemented in waveguide and ring resonator systems, where spatial modulation emulates temporal periodicity41–43; such setups inherently exclude harmonic generation due to their time-invariant nature.

Here, we introduce and experimentally observe a new type of NHSE, dubbed harmonic NHSE, in Floquet non-Hermitian lattices. This phenomenon results from a direct synergy between Floquet engineering and non-Hermitian topology—time-periodic driving generates a spectrum of harmonics in open-boundary lattices, while the skin localization of each harmonic is dictated by the spectral winding topology at its own frequency. The concept is demonstrated through a simple Hatano-Nelson (HN) model44 incorporating time-periodic couplings. In addition to the unipolar harmonic NHSE induced by uniform spectral winding, more intriguingly, as sketched in Fig. 1, the harmonics can exhibit bipolar NHSE in a long-range lattice with twisted winding spectrum, despite the extended nature of the fundamental wave. Experimentally, we design two nonreciprocal acoustic lattices to observe these harmonic NHSEs, with both dynamic and nonreciprocal couplings reconfigurable via active unidirectional couplers. By tuning the excitation and modulation frequencies, we clearly demonstrate the ability of selectively localizing different harmonics, with their weights flexibly controllable by simply adjusting the duty ratio of dynamic couplings. These results not only extend the existing NHSE framework but also open new avenues for harmonic wave manipulation.

In this manuscript, Zhang et al. introduce and experimentally demonstrate the concept of a
"harmonic non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE)" in a Floquet-engineered acoustic lattice. The core idea
is that when a monochromatic wave excites a time-periodically modulated non-Hermitian lattice,
it can generate multiple harmonics, each of which can exhibit a distinct skin localization
phenotype—unipolar or bipolar—dictated by the spectral winding topology at its respective
frequency. The authors provide a theoretical framework based on a frequency-domain analysis and
present compelling experimental evidence using a reconfigurable acoustic platform with active,
real-time modulations. The ability to selectively control and spatially separate different harmonic
components via a single-frequency excitation is a key experimental achievement.
I find this work to be of high quality, timely, and highly suitable for publication in Nature
Communications. The concept of "harmonic NHSE" is novel and represents a significant extension
of the non-Hermitian skin effect into the realm of Floquet systems with genuine time modulation.
The study successfully bridges a gap in the field by focusing on the harmonic generation aspect,
which is a fundamental feature of Floquet systems but had been overlooked in previous studies of
Floquet NHSE, particularly those relying on synthetic dimensions (e.g., waveguide arrays). The
combination of a clear theoretical proposal with a sophisticated and convincing experimental
demonstration in acoustics is a major strength. The observation of both unipolar and, more
impressively, bipolar harmonic NHSE, where different harmonics localize at opposite ends of the
system, is a striking result. The findings are likely to stimulate immediate interest across various
platforms in photonics, circuit QED, and cold atoms.
I am therefore strongly in favor of publication, provided that the authors can address the following
points to further enhance the clarity and theoretical rigor of their otherwise excellent manuscript.

coupling, giving the well-known unipolar NHSE [Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 570 (1996)]. However, in more

circle correspond to exponential localization toward the left (right) boundary.

## Paper

## Abstract

The non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), an exotic phenomenon of localization at the boundary, has recently drawn extensive attention and Floquet engineering offers a powerful approach to expanding its scope. The fundamental role of harmonic response in Floquet systems has nonetheless yet to be elucidated. Here, we introduce the concept of harmonic NHSE and demonstrate it experimentally in an acoustic platform. Within our theoretical framework, we demonstrate that incorporating dynamic couplings into the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model causes a single-frequency input to generate multiple harmonics with diverse skin morphologies, each dictated by the underlying spectral winding topology at its respective frequency. Experimentally, we implement the requisite dynamic couplings in an acoustic lattice via programmable unidirectional couplers. By simply reconfiguring the excitation and modulation frequencies, we demonstrate controllable switching of unipolar and bipolar harmonic NHSEs, which exhibit uniform and opposite sound gathering toward the sample boundaries, respectively. By introducing the class of harmonic NHSE, our work sets the stage for further investigating non-Hermitian physics with harmonic effects.

---

## Introduction

Non-Hermitian systems, typically featuring asymmetric couplings and gain/loss, have garnered extensive attention owing to their unique phenomena and broad applications beyond Hermitian regimes1–3. In particular, the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), referring to the accumulation of bulk states at the lattice boundary, has emerged as a cornerstone of non-Hermitian physics4–6. Over the past few years, a number of theoretical frameworks, such as the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ), Bloch spectral winding and dynamical degeneracy splitting, have been developed to characterize the NHSE and its related topological properties7–14. These advances have propelled the experimental observation of diverse NHSE morphologies across photonic15, circuit16,17, acoustic18–21, mechanical22,23, quantum walk24, and ultracold atom25,26 platforms, paving the way for potential applications in optical funneling15, robust directional transport27, and non-Hermitian lasing28.

Floquet engineering, an established approach for tailoring material properties via time-periodic modulation29–31, has recently been extended to non-Hermitian systems. This development has led to richer phenomena, including non-Hermitian Floquet topological states32–34, multiple phase transitions35,36, and Floquet exceptional points37,38. In particular, a periodically driven system can exhibit Floquet NHSE even when the instantaneous Hamiltonian at each step lacks NHSE38–43. Along with breaking the bulk-boundary correspondence, Floquet NHSE enables the relocation of topological edge states to a single boundary or the separation of distinct edge states at opposite boundaries, giving rise to the Floquet skin-topological effect40,41. In these studies, the key roles played by Floquet engineering are breaking time-reversal symmetry and introducing artificial gauge fields (or complex long-range couplings). Despite these advances, however, the implications of harmonic generation—a fundamental feature of Floquet systems—has yet to be explored in the context of NHSE. The primary reasons are twofold. Theoretically, most studies focus on the stroboscopic dynamics governed by the effective Hamiltonian38–40; the higher-order Floquet states (harmonics), which share the same eigen-properties with the zeroth-order one, are typically disregarded. Experimentally, Floquet NHSE has so far been implemented in waveguide and ring resonator systems, where spatial modulation emulates temporal periodicity41–43; such setups inherently exclude harmonic generation due to their time-invariant nature.

Here, we introduce and experimentally observe a new type of NHSE, dubbed harmonic NHSE, in Floquet non-Hermitian lattices. This phenomenon results from a direct synergy between Floquet engineering and non-Hermitian topology—time-periodic driving generates a spectrum of harmonics in open-boundary lattices, while the skin localization of each harmonic is dictated by the spectral winding topology at its own frequency. The concept is demonstrated through a simple Hatano-Nelson (HN) model44 incorporating time-periodic couplings. In addition to the unipolar harmonic NHSE induced by uniform spectral winding, more intriguingly, as sketched in Fig. 1, the harmonics can exhibit bipolar NHSE in a long-range lattice with twisted winding spectrum, despite the extended nature of the fundamental wave. Experimentally, we design two nonreciprocal acoustic lattices to observe these harmonic NHSEs, with both dynamic and nonreciprocal couplings reconfigurable via active unidirectional couplers. By tuning the excitation and modulation frequencies, we clearly demonstrate the ability of selectively localizing different harmonics, with their weights flexibly controllable by simply adjusting the duty ratio of dynamic couplings. These results not only extend the existing NHSE framework but also open new avenues for harmonic wave manipulation.

## Results

In contrast to the above eigenvalue problem, in practice, one needs to consider an excitation problem to identify the harmonic NHSE. Given the real-space Hamiltonian H r (t) for an N-site finite lattice with open boundaries, the response to a monochromatic excitation at frequency f 0 is described by (see Methods):

(Δ 0 +mΩ) Q m + Δ 1 Q m-1 + Δ -1 Q m+1 = P m (1)

where Δ m = T 1 T 0 H k (t)ei2mπΩtdt is the mth-order Fourier component of H k (t), with Ω = 1/T denoting the modulation frequency. In particular, Δ 0 = T 1 T 0 H k (t)dt = H(cid:2) k denotes the time-averaged Hamiltonian. The spectrum of H k under periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) comprises infinitely many branches, each shifted by Ω, as a result of the unitary transformation UyH k U = diag(H(cid:2) k+mΩ, ..., H(cid:2) k+Ω, H(cid:2) k, H(cid:2) k-Ω, ..., H(cid:2) k-mΩ)45. Due to the single-band nature of our model, these spectral branches remain non-interacting even when they overlap, unlike in two- or multi-band cases46. Specifically, the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k corresponds to that of H(cid:2) k - mΩ, and its winding topology governs the NHSE under open boundary conditions (OBCs) within the associated Floquet replica.

Moreover, as demonstrated above, the NHSE within the mth-order Floquet replica is governed by the mth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently by the spectrum of H(cid:2) k - mΩ. Consequently, the harmonic NHSE under realistic excitation can be fully characterized by examining solely the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k, or equivalently, the spectrum of H(cid:2) k for single-band models. (Remarkably, for two- or multi-band models, the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k can differ fundamentally from the spectrum of H(cid:2) k, due to the interaction between different Floquet branches upon closing46). The above theoretical framework provides a general route to account for harmonic effects in Floquet non-Hermitian systems.

First, we introduce time-periodic dynamic couplings into a prototypical static HN lattice44, forming a Floquet HN (FHN) lattice (see Fig. 2a). The Bloch Hamiltonian of the FHN lattice is H k (t) = κ L + κ D (t) eik + κ R + κ D (t) e-ik. Physically, the nonreciprocal static couplings κ L and κ R establish the fundamental NHSE, while the reciprocal dynamic couplings κ D (t) contribute to the harmonic generation. For simplicity, we assume κ D (t) = κ 0 cos(2πΩt), as it couples only Floquet harmonics of adjacent orders without introducing any additional static component. As shown in Fig. 2b, both the spectrum of H(cid:2) k and the zeroth-order Floquet spectrum of H k form a counterclockwise loop in the complex frequency plane. A reference frequency f b enclosed by the spectrum f(k) carries a nontrivial spectral winding number and their associated NHSEs. Specifically, when choosing the excitation frequency f 0 = 0 and modulation frequency Ω = 1.5, the fundamental frequency f 0 lies at the Bloch-like point of the spectrum, while the +1st- and -1st-order harmonic frequencies f +1 and f -1 fall within the counterclockwise and clockwise spectral loops, respectively (see Fig. 2e). Protected by the twisted winding topology, the incident fundamental wave maintains an extended spatial distribution, whereas the +1st- and -1st-order harmonics undergo unidirectional accumulation toward the left and right boundaries, respectively, as shown in Fig. 2f. Notably, the extended nature at the Bloch-like point can be interpreted in terms of both the vanishing spectral winding number and the specific GBZ with purely real Bloch wave vectors4,8. Furthermore, different harmonics can be selectively engineered to exhibit distinct skin and evanescent behaviors by tuning f 0 and Ω, as detailed in Supplementary Note 2.

We further achieve control over the harmonic intensity distribution by tuning the duty ratio R of dynamic couplings. Since the Fourier components of the dynamic couplings determine the conversion between harmonics, varying R effectively modulates their magnitudes and thereby tailors the intensity weights of individual harmonics within the lattice. This controllability is readily implemented by leveraging the flexible tunability of the real-time unidirectional couplers in our experiments. To ensure that the PBC spectra of time-averaged Hamiltonians (and hence the harmonic NHSE) remain quantitatively unchanged during variation of R, we keep the zeroth-order Fourier component of κ D constant, namely, Rκ 0 = κ(cid:2). Under this condition, the coefficient of the leading order (±1st) Fourier component of κ D is given by c ±1 = ±κ(cid:2)sinc(πR), whose absolute value decreases monotonically with increasing R in the interval [0, 1]. Specifically, when R approaches zero, c ±1 reaches its maximum value κ(cid:2); when R approaches one, c ±1 decreases to its minimum value zero.

The combination of a clear theoretical proposal with a sophisticated and convincing experimental demonstration in acoustics is a major strength. The observation of both unipolar and, more impressively, bipolar harmonic NHSE, where different harmonics localize at opposite ends of the system, is a striking result. The findings are likely to stimulate immediate interest across various platforms in photonics, circuit QED, and cold atoms.

In this manuscript, Zhang et al. introduce and experimentally demonstrate the concept of a
"harmonic non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE)" in a Floquet-engineered acoustic lattice. The core idea
is that when a monochromatic wave excites a time-periodically modulated non-Hermitian lattice,
it can generate multiple harmonics, each of which can exhibit a distinct skin localization
phenotype—unipolar or bipolar—dictated by the spectral winding topology at its respective
frequency. The authors provide a theoretical framework based on a frequency-domain analysis and
present compelling experimental evidence using a reconfigurable acoustic platform with active,
real-time modulations. The ability to selectively control and spatially separate different harmonic
components via a single-frequency excitation is a key experimental achievement.
I find this work to be of high quality, timely, and highly suitable for publication in Nature
Communications. The concept of "harmonic NHSE" is novel and represents a significant extension
of the non-Hermitian skin effect into the realm of Floquet systems with genuine time modulation.
The study successfully bridges a gap in the field by focusing on the harmonic generation aspect,
which is a fundamental feature of Floquet systems but had been overlooked in previous studies of
Floquet NHSE, particularly those relying on synthetic dimensions (e.g., waveguide arrays). The
combination of a clear theoretical proposal with a sophisticated and convincing experimental
demonstration in acoustics is a major strength. The observation of both unipolar and, more
impressively, bipolar harmonic NHSE, where different harmonics localize at opposite ends of the
system, is a striking result. The findings are likely to stimulate immediate interest across various
platforms in photonics, circuit QED, and cold atoms.
I am therefore strongly in favor of publication, provided that the authors can address the following
points to further enhance the clarity and theoretical rigor of their otherwise excellent manuscript.

2. Clarification on the Extended Nature of the Zeroth Harmonic (f₀): In Figure 1 and the

The authors should provide a clearer explanation for this observation. Is this extended behavior a result
of a specific parameter choice (e.g., f₀ being exactly at a Bloch-like point in the spectrum)? A
detailed discussion on why f₀ resists skin localization in this specific scenario, while the system

Reply: This is an insightful question. First, we confirm that the zeroth-order harmonic f₀ in bipolar
harmonic NHSE is indeed chosen to lie exactly at a Bloch-like point of the spectrum. Below we
explain why a Bloch-like point corresponds to an extended state despite the underlying
nonreciprocal couplings. In simple settings such as the Hatano–Nelson model with nearest-
neighbor nonreciprocal couplings, all eigenstates localize toward the direction of the dominant
coupling, giving the well-known unipolar NHSE [Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 570 (1996)]. However, in more
complex settings—e.g., when long-range nonreciprocal couplings are introduced—the situation
becomes richer. Besides the majority of eigenstates that exhibit leftward and rightward NHSE
(bipolar NHSE), there can exist isolated extended eigenstates, whose eigenenergies exactly
correspond to the Bloch-like points [Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 246801 (2019); Phys. Rev. Res. 1, 023013
(2019)]. These points and the associated bipolar NHSE defy the oversimplified picture in which all
eigenstates localize toward the dominant hopping direction. These Bloch-like extended states can
be understood from two complementary perspectives. 1) Spectral winding perspective: A Bloch-
like point is an eigenenergy at which the periodic boundary condition (PBC) spectrum intersects
the open boundary condition (OBC) spectrum (see Fig. R5a). Its PBC spectral winding number is
therefore zero, unlike the majority of eigenenergies that carry a nonzero winding number.
According to the topological origin of the NHSE [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 086801 (2020); Phys. Rev. Lett.
125, 126402 (2020)], only eigenstates associated with nonzero winding undergo skin localization.
The Bloch-like eigenstate, having zero winding, remains extended. 2) GBZ perspective: At a Bloch-
like point, the GBZ intersects the unit circle, meaning that the corresponding Bloch wave vector is
purely real (see Fig. R5b). As a result, the wave function is spatially extended [Phys. Rev. Lett. 121,
086803 (2018)]. In contrast, the bipolar NHSE emerges because points inside (outside) the unit
circle correspond to exponential localization toward the left (right) boundary.

vanishing spectral winding number and the specific GBZ with purely real Bloch wave vectors4,8.”
